gloss: flesh, meat, body; mankind, all that lives; bring news, herald
summary: Two families of words share the root. The noun בָּשָׂר is flesh: the soft substance of a living body over the bones and under the skin, meat as food and in sacrifice, the body as a whole, a man's own kin (“my bone and my flesh”), and “all flesh”, every creature that breathes, above all mankind, frail and mortal before God who is spirit (Isa 31:3; 40:6). The verb בִּשֵּׂר, used only in the piel and once in the hithpael, is to bring news, the runner's word from the battle, good or bad, and in the prophets the herald who tells Zion “Your God reigns” (Isa 52:7); its noun בְּשֹׂרָה is the news, or the reward for bringing it. Arabic keeps both in one root, bašar “skin; mankind” and baššara “bring news”, and its lexicographers explain the news as what changes the hearer's skin, his face; scripture itself does not show how the two meanings meet.

words.gloss: flesh, meat; body; kin; all flesh, mankind
words.summary: About 270 times. Flesh with bones, sinews and skin is the stuff of a living body (Job 10:11; Ezk 37:6–8); the same word is meat on the table and on the altar. Flesh also stands for the whole man in his body, for his kin, and, in “all flesh”, for every living creature, often mankind as weak and mortal set against God and against spirit.

senses.definition: The soft substance of a man's or a beast's body, with bone, sinew and skin; it can be fat or lean, sound or diseased, and is what wastes away or is restored.

evidence.note: Yahweh God took one of the man's ribs “and closed up the place with flesh (בָּשָׂר) in its stead”.
“With skin and flesh (עוֹר וּבָשָׂר) you clothed me, and with bones and sinews you knit me together.”
On the dry bones “sinews, and flesh came up, and skin covered them above, but there was no breath in them”.
“My bone cleaves to my skin and to my flesh.”
“By the sound of my groaning my bone cleaves to my flesh.”
The leprous hand put back into his bosom “was restored like his flesh”.
Naaman dipped in the Jordan, “and his flesh returned like the flesh of a little boy, and he was clean”.
“Like a dead one … half his flesh eaten away”.
A swelling “in the skin of his flesh”: the laws of skin disease.
“His flesh becomes fresher than a child's; he returns to the days of his youth.”
Seven cows “fair of appearance and fat of flesh (בְּרִיאֹת בָּשָׂר)”, against the seven “lean of flesh” (v. 19).
Daniel and his friends looked better “and fatter in flesh” than those who ate the king's food.
“My knees stumble from fasting, and my flesh has grown lean, without fat.”
“The birds will eat your flesh from on you.”
The rulers “eat the flesh of my people, and strip their skin from on them, and break their bones”: flesh, skin and bones of a people devoured.

senses.definition: The flesh cut in circumcision, the sign of the covenant; “uncircumcised in flesh” is said of foreigners beside “uncircumcised in heart”.

evidence.note: “You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin (בְּשַׂר עָרְלַתְכֶם), and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.”
“My covenant shall be in your flesh for an everlasting covenant.”
“Sons of a foreigner, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh (עַרְלֵי בָשָׂר).”

senses.gloss: meat, as food and in sacrifice
senses.definition: The flesh of beasts eaten as food, longed for or given, set beside bread; and the flesh of an offering, eaten by priest and offerer or burned, never with its blood.

evidence.note: “When we sat by the pots of meat (סִיר הַבָּשָׂר), when we ate bread to the full.”
“Who will give us meat (בָּשָׂר) to eat?”
“Yahweh will give you meat, and you shall eat.”
“While the meat was still between their teeth”.
The ravens brought Elijah “bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening”.
When the border is enlarged and you say “I will eat meat”, because your soul desires to eat meat, you may eat it.
“Only flesh with its soul, its blood, you shall not eat.”
“They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted with fire, with unleavened bread.”
Flesh of the peace offering that touches anything unclean is burned; “as for the flesh, everyone clean may eat flesh”.
Eli's servant demands raw “flesh to roast for the priest” before the fat is burned.
The flesh of the bull of the sin offering, its skin and its dung, burned outside the camp.
“Holy flesh (בְּשַׂר־קֹדֶשׁ) in the fold of his garment”.
“Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?”
“Eating flesh and drinking wine: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
“Who eat the flesh of the pig”.
Daniel's mourning: “neither flesh nor wine came into my mouth”.
Yahweh's sacrifice on the mountains of Israel: “you shall eat flesh and drink blood”.
“That you may eat the flesh (σάρκας) of kings …”, the supper of Ezk 39:17–20.

senses.gloss: body; the man in his body
senses.definition: The whole body, washed, clothed or cut; and the man himself as a bodily creature, set beside his heart or soul, who longs, rejoices, rests or wearies.

evidence.note: Linen undergarments “shall be on his flesh … and he shall bathe his flesh in water”.
“You shall not make cuttings in your flesh for a soul.”
“My soul (נַפְשִׁי) thirsts for you, my flesh (בְשָׂרִי) longs for you, in a dry and weary land.”
“My heart and my flesh sing for joy to the living God.”
“My heart is glad and my glory rejoices; my flesh also will dwell in safety.”
“Only his flesh grieves for him, and his soul mourns for him.”
“The hair of my flesh stood up.”
“A heart of healing is the life of the flesh (חַיֵּי בְשָׂרִים), but envy is rot of the bones.”
“Much study is a weariness of the flesh.”
“Touch his bone and his flesh”: the man himself in his body.

senses.definition: With a discharge, or with “nakedness”, the flesh is the genitals, of a man or a woman.

evidence.note: “When any man has a discharge from his flesh (מִבְּשָׂרוֹ), his discharge is unclean.”
Of a woman: “her discharge in her flesh is blood”.
Linen breeches “to cover the flesh of nakedness (בְּשַׂר עֶרְוָה)”.
Jerusalem's harlotry with the Egyptians, “great of flesh”.

senses.definition: A man's relatives are his own flesh, “my bone and my flesh”: the woman taken from the man, a brother, a clan, a tribe, a whole people; a man and his wife become one flesh.

evidence.note: “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she was taken out of man.”
“A man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh (לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד).”
Jesus quotes Gen 2:24: “they are no longer two but one flesh (σὰρξ μία)”; the Peshitta reads חַדֿ בּסַר.
Laban to Jacob: “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.”
“Let our hand not be on him, for he is our brother, our flesh.”
Abimelech to Shechem, his mother's town: “remember that I am your bone and your flesh”.
All the tribes of Israel to David: “Behold, we are your bone and your flesh.”
“None of you shall approach any near kin of his flesh (שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ).”
A kinsman of his flesh, of his clan, may redeem him.
“Our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children as their children.”
“And not hide yourself from your own flesh.”

senses.gloss: all flesh: every living creature; mankind
senses.definition: “All flesh” is every creature with the breath of life, beast and man together; most often mankind, all peoples, who are fed by God, judged by him, and will see his glory and worship before him.

evidence.note: “To destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life (רוּחַ חַיִּים) from under heaven; everything on the earth shall die.”
“All flesh that moved on the earth died, birds, cattle, beasts … and every man.”
“All flesh had corrupted its way on the earth.”
“Never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood.”
“God, the God of the spirits of all flesh”.
“Who gives bread to all flesh, for his steadfast love is for ever.”
“Let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever.”
“You who hear prayer, to you all flesh shall come.”
“The glory of Yahweh shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together.” Luke quotes it of the coming of the Christ (Luk 3:6).
“All flesh shall know that I, Yahweh, am your saviour.”
“All flesh shall come to worship before me.”
“He enters into judgment with all flesh.”
“I am Yahweh, the God of all flesh; is anything too hard for me?”
“I will pour out my spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.” Quoted by Peter at Pentecost (Act 2:17).
“Be silent, all flesh, before Yahweh.”
“All flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust.”

senses.gloss: flesh: man as weak and mortal
senses.definition: Man as flesh, set against God and against spirit: frail, passing like a wind or like grass, no ground for trust.

evidence.note: “My spirit shall not abide in man for ever, for he is flesh; his days shall be a hundred and twenty years.”
“The Egyptians are man and not God (אָדָם וְלֹא־אֵל), and their horses flesh and not spirit (בָּשָׂר וְלֹא־רוּחַ).”
“He remembered that they were flesh, a wind that goes and does not return.”
“All flesh is grass, and all its steadfastness like the flower of the field”; the grass withers, “but the word of our God will stand for ever” (v. 8). Quoted at 1Pe 1:24–25.
“Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart turns from Yahweh.”
Hezekiah of Sennacherib: “With him is an arm of flesh (זְרוֹעַ בָּשָׂר), but with us is Yahweh our God to help us.”
“In God I trust; I will not fear. What can flesh do to me?”
“Have you eyes of flesh? Or do you see as man sees?”

senses.definition: A living, responsive heart that Yahweh gives in place of a heart of stone, with a new spirit, so that his people keep his statutes.

evidence.note: “I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh (לֵב בָּשָׂר).”
The same promise, “one heart” and “a new spirit”, that they may walk in my statutes (v. 20).

evidence.locator: Gen.2.24, בָשָׂר → σάρκα; Gen.6.12, בָּשָׂר → σὰρξ; Isa.40.6, בָּשָׂר → σὰρξ; σάρξ renders בָּשָׂר ×123

evidence.note: “The two shall become one flesh”: Gen 2:24.
“I will pour out my spirit on all flesh”: Jol 3:1.
“All flesh is as grass”: Isa 40:6.
“All flesh shall see the salvation of God”: Isa 40:5.
“Neither did his flesh see corruption”: Psa 16:9–10 of the risen Christ.

evidence.locator: Exo.16.3, בָּשָׂר → κρεῶν; Num.11.4, בָּשָׂר → κρέα; κρέας renders בָּשָׂר ×69

evidence.note: “It is good not to eat meat (κρέα) or drink wine.”

parallels.note: Bone with flesh: the whole body, and the bond of kinship (“my bone and my flesh”).
Soul and flesh side by side: the whole living man.
Heart and flesh: the inner man and his body together.

opposites.note: Flesh is not spirit: horses are flesh, God is spirit; the spirit of Yahweh does not abide with man for ever, for he is flesh.
Man and not God (Isa 31:3); flesh against God in whom the psalmist trusts.
A heart of stone against a heart of flesh.

phrases.gloss: all flesh: every living creature, all mankind
my bone and my flesh: my kin
the kin of his flesh, near relative
an arm of flesh: human strength

words.summary: Daniel's Aramaic, three times, with the Hebrew noun's meanings: meat eaten, all that lives, and mankind as distinct from gods.

senses.definition: Flesh eaten by a beast of prey.

evidence.note: The second beast, like a bear, is told “Arise, devour much flesh (בְּשַׂר שַׂגִּיא).”

senses.definition: All that lives, fed from the great tree of Nebuchadnezzar's dream.

evidence.note: Beasts under it, birds in its branches, “and from it all flesh (כָּל־בִּשְׂרָא) was fed”.

senses.definition: Men, among whom the gods do not dwell.

evidence.note: The Chaldeans: no one can tell the dream “except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh (עִם־בִּשְׂרָא)”.

words.summary: The Peshitta's word for flesh, about 120 verses, for σάρξ: the body of flesh and bones, “flesh and blood” for man, and “all flesh” for mankind. In Jhn 6:51–56 it uses פַּגרָא “body” instead.

senses.definition: The substance of a living body, with bones, which a spirit does not have; and the body of the Son, in which he condemned sin.

evidence.note: The risen Jesus: “a spirit has no flesh (בֵּסרָא) and bones, as you see that I have.”
“And the word became flesh (בֵּסרָא) and dwelt among us.”
God sent his Son “in the likeness of the flesh of sin (בַּדֿמֻותָֿא דּבֵֿסרָא דַּחטִיתָֿא) … and condemned sin in his flesh”.
“The two of them shall be one flesh (חַדֿ בּסַר)”: Gen 2:24.

senses.gloss: flesh and blood; all flesh: man, mankind
senses.definition: Man as mortal flesh: “flesh and blood”, which cannot reveal the Christ nor inherit the kingdom, and which the children and the Son share; and “all flesh”, all mankind.

evidence.note: “Flesh and blood (בֵּסרָא וַדֿמָא) has not revealed it to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”
“Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of heaven, nor does corruption inherit incorruption.”
“Since the children share in flesh and blood, he also himself in like manner shared in the same.”
“What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit.”
“All flesh (כֻּל בּסַר) shall see the life of God”: Isa 40:5.
“I will pour out my spirit on all flesh”: Jol 3:1.
“All flesh is grass”: Isa 40:6.

words.gloss: bring news; herald, proclaim; (hithpael) receive news
words.summary: Piel only, with one hithpael: 24 times. The messenger who runs from a battle with word of it is the מְבַשֵּׂר, and what he brings may be defeat and death (1Sa 4:17), so that “good” is added when the news is good (1Ki 1:42; 2Sa 18:27). In the Psalms and Isaiah the herald proclaims Yahweh's salvation, his righteousness, and his reign in Zion. How the verb is tied to בָּשָׂר “flesh” scripture does not show; see the root's summary and the Arabic cognates.

senses.definition: To bring word of an event to one who waits for it, most often a runner from a battle; the news may be welcome or bitter, and the bringer looks for a reward.

evidence.note: “The one bringing news (הַמְבַשֵּׂר) answered: Israel has fled before the Philistines … your two sons are dead, and the ark of God is taken.” News of defeat.
Ahimaaz: “Let me run and bring the king news (וַאֲבַשְּׂרָה) that Yahweh has judged him from the hand of his enemies.”
Joab: “You are not a man of news (אִישׁ בְּשֹׂרָה) today; you shall bring news another day, but today you shall not bring news, because the king's son is dead.”
The king, seeing a man running alone: “He too brings news.”
The man who told David “Saul is dead” “was in his own eyes like one bringing news (כִמְבַשֵּׂר)”, and David killed him “who thought I would give him a reward for news (בְּשֹׂרָה)”.
Adonijah to Jonathan: “Come in, for you are a worthy man and bring good news (וְטוֹב תְּבַשֵּׂר)”; the news was that Solomon was king.
“Tell it not in Gath, announce it not (אַל־תְּבַשְּׂרוּ) in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice”; parallel הִגִּיד “tell”.
The Philistines sent round their land “to announce it in the house of their idols and to the people”.
“Cursed be the man who brought news (בִּשַּׂר) to my father, saying, A son is born to you, making him very glad.”

senses.definition: To proclaim publicly what Yahweh has done and will do: his salvation, righteousness and praises, and above all, by the herald to Zion, that Yahweh comes and reigns; the anointed one is sent to proclaim it to the poor.

evidence.note: “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of the herald (מְבַשֵּׂר), who makes peace heard, who heralds good (מְבַשֵּׂר טוֹב), who makes salvation heard, who says to Zion, Your God reigns (מָלַךְ אֱלֹהָיִךְ)!”
Paul quotes Isa 52:7 of the preachers of the word of faith; the Peshitta writes דַּמסַבּרַי שלָמָא.
“Go up on a high mountain, herald of Zion (מְבַשֶּׂרֶת צִיּוֹן) … lift up your voice with strength … say to the cities of Judah, Behold your God!”
“I give to Jerusalem a herald.”
“Behold on the mountains the feet of a herald, who makes peace heard!” at the fall of Nineveh.

“The spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me, because Yahweh has anointed me to proclaim good news to the humble (לְבַשֵּׂר עֲנָוִים); he has sent me to bind up the broken-hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives.”
Jesus reads Isa 61:1 in the synagogue at Nazareth (εὐαγγελίσασθαι; Peshitta לַמסַבָּרֻו) and says, “Today this scripture is fulfilled in your ears.”
“The poor have good news proclaimed to them”: Isa 61:1, as the sign that he is the one who comes.
From Sheba they bring gold and frankincense “and proclaim the praises of Yahweh”.
“I have proclaimed righteousness (בִּשַּׂרְתִּי צֶדֶק) in the great congregation; behold, I did not restrain my lips.”
“Sing to Yahweh, bless his name; proclaim his salvation from day to day”, and “say among the nations, Yahweh reigns … for he comes to judge the earth” (vv. 10, 13).
“The Lord gives the word; the women who proclaim it are a great host.”

senses.definition: To have news brought to one.

evidence.note: The Cushite: “Let my lord the king receive the news (יִתְבַּשֵּׂר) that Yahweh has judged you this day from the hand of all who rose against you.”

greek.gloss: bring good news, preach the gospel

evidence.locator: Isa.52.7, מְבַשֵּׂר → εὐαγγελιζομένου; Isa.61.1, בַשֵּׂר → εὐαγγελίσασθαι; Psa.96.2, בַּשְּׂרוּ → εὐαγγελίζεσθε; 2Sa.18.26, מְבַשֵּׂר → εὐαγγελιζόμενος

evidence.note: Isa 61:1 read and fulfilled.
Isa 52:7 quoted.
“I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also.”
Philip “proclaiming the good news concerning the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ”.
The scripture “proclaimed the good news beforehand (προευηγγελίσατο) to Abraham, In you shall all the nations be blessed”.

words.summary: Six times, all in the stories of runners bringing news to a king. It is news as such: Joab can say the day's news is unfit for Ahimaaz, and the king adds “good” when he hopes it is (2Sa 18:27). It is also the reward given for bringing it (2Sa 4:10).

senses.definition: Word of what has happened, brought to one who must hear it.

evidence.note: “If he is alone, there is news (בְּשׂוֹרָה) in his mouth.”
“He is a good man, and comes with good news (בְּשׂוֹרָה טוֹבָה).”
“You are not a man of news today.”
The lepers who found the Syrian camp empty: “This day is a day of news (יוֹם בְּשֹׂרָה), and we are keeping silent … let us go and tell the king's household.”

senses.definition: What the bringer of news is given for it.

evidence.note: David killed the man who brought word of Saul's death, “to whom I should have given a reward for news (לְתִתִּי־לוֹ בְּשֹׂרָה)”.
Joab to Ahimaaz: “Why will you run, my son, seeing you will have no news that finds anything (אֵין־בְּשׂוֹרָה מֹצֵאת)?”: news that brings no reward.

evidence.locator: 2Sa.4.10, בְּשֹׂרָה → εὐαγγέλια; elsewhere εὐαγγελία (2Sa.18.20, 22, 25, 27; 2Ki.7.9)

evidence.note: “Jesus came into Galilee proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom of God, and saying, The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God has drawn near; repent and believe in the gospel.” The Peshitta writes סבַֿרתָֿא.
“This gospel of the kingdom shall be proclaimed in all the world.”
“An everlasting gospel to proclaim to those who dwell on the earth.”

words.summary: The wadi south of Ziklag, always נַחַל הַבְּשׂוֹר with the article, where two hundred of David's men, too faint to cross, stayed with the baggage while he pursued the Amalekites. Its spelling is the root's, but nothing in the text says what it was named for, so its tie to “flesh” or to “news” is not shown; it names no cognate and the evidence table counts the root's cognates against it. A place, so it has no name entry.

senses.definition: A wadi on David's route from Ziklag after the Amalekites.

evidence.note: David and six hundred men “came to the wadi Besor (נַחַל הַבְּשׂוֹר), where those left behind stayed”.

cognates.gloss: outer skin, epidermis, of a human being; mankind, a human being; (verb bašara) pare a hide
cognates.note: The Arabic noun is the skin, the surface of the body, and by extension mankind, “a human being”, as Hebrew “all flesh”. Arabic š answers Hebrew שׂ as regularly. The third stem bāšara “be in contact skin to skin; lie with (a woman)” (Lane n2590) is near the Hebrew's euphemistic use of flesh.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 208, art. بشر, بَشَرَةٌ (n2597)
evidence.note: “The external skin; the cuticle, or scarf-skin; the epidermis; the exterior of the skin of a human being … that which is next the flesh.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 208, art. بشر, بَشَرٌ (n2596)
evidence.note: “Mankind: and the human being: applied to the male and to the female; and used alike as sing. and pl.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 207, art. بشر, بَشَرَ (n2588)
evidence.note: “He pared a hide, removing its بَشَرَة.”

evidence.locator: SEM000026 bśr [flesh] N, ARB001810 ba$ar [Mankind]

cognates.gloss: announce to someone an event, mostly joyful but also grievous; (bašīr, mubaššir) one who announces
cognates.note: The same Arabic root as bašar “skin”. The lexicographers Lane cites explain the verb as announcing “an event which produced a change in his بَشَرَة [complexion]”, and so a joyful event, but also one that grieves; the Hebrew verb likewise carries news of defeat (1Sa 4:17) as well as victory. This is the Arabs' own account of how the two meanings meet, not scripture's.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 207, art. بشر, بشّرهُ (n2589)
evidence.note: “Originally signifying He announced to him an event which produced a change in his بَشَرَة [or complexion]: and hence, he announced to him an event which rejoiced him … and he announced to him an event which grieved him.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 208, art. بشر, بَشِيرٌ (n2603)
evidence.note: “One who announces to a people [or person] an event, either good or evil; but meaning the former oftener than the latter.”

evidence.locator: Arabic بشر (baššara), verb, etymology 3
evidence.note: “To bring good news (to)”; cognate with Hebrew בִּשֵּׂר.

cognates.gloss: good news, joyful tidings; a gift to the one who announces a joyful event
cognates.note: Both the news and the reward for it, as the Hebrew בְּשֹׂרָה is both (2Sa 18:27; 2Sa 4:10).

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 208, art. بشر, بُشْرَى (n2598)
evidence.note: “A joyful annunciation; joyful, or glad, tidings; good news.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 208, art. بشر, بِشَارَةٌ (n2606)
evidence.note: “Also A gift to him who announces a joyful event … I gave him my garment as a reward for the joyful annunciation.”

evidence.locator: SEM000026 bśr [flesh] N, UGC001295 bšr [flesh] N
Phoenician 𐤁𐤔𐤓 (bšr), noun
evidence.note: “Meat; flesh”, from Proto-West Semitic *baśar-.

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic of the Targums and Talmud. The Targum of Jer 17:5 uses it for the Hebrew “flesh” a man makes his arm, in the sense “mortal”.

evidence.locator: s.v. בִּשְׂרָא (B01372), citing Targ. Gen. II, 21; Targ. Lev. XIII, 2 (body, flesh, meat); Targ. Jer. XVII, 5 (mortal)

cognates.gloss: (pael) bring good tidings; (ithpaal) receive good tidings; be glad
cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic; the Targum of Jer 20:15 uses the pael for the Hebrew piel “brought news to my father”.

evidence.locator: s.v. בְּשַׂר (B01369), Pa. Targ. Jer. XX, 15; Ithpa. Targ. Ruth I, 6

cognates.gloss: bring a message, bring good news
cognates.note: Neo-Assyrian, often spelled with p (upassar, passir). Akkadian has no cognate “flesh” in Oracc's glossaries; its word is šīru.

cognates.note: The Peshitta's verb and noun for εὐαγγελίζω and εὐαγγέλιον (Luk 4:18; Rom 10:15; Mrk 1:14–15). If it is בשׂר with the first two letters exchanged, it is the root's own verb in the Peshitta; but SEDRA files it under a root ܣܒܪ beside ܣܒܪ “think, hope”, so the tie is argued, not shown.

doctrine.statement: Man is called flesh because he is mortal: “My spirit shall not abide in man for ever, for he is flesh; his days shall be a hundred and twenty years” (Gen 6:3). Yahweh “remembered that they were flesh, a wind that goes and does not return” (Psa 78:39); “if he gathered to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together, and man would return to dust” (Job 34:14–15). The flood destroyed “all flesh in which is the breath of life”, man with the beasts (Gen 6:17; 7:21–22). The life of flesh is not a separate thing within it but its blood: “the soul (נֶפֶשׁ) of the flesh is in the blood”, so that flesh is not to be eaten “with its soul, its blood” (Lev 17:11, 14; Gen 9:4). “All flesh is grass … the grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand for ever” (Isa 40:6–8), which Peter applies to the word preached to believers, by which they are born again of incorruptible seed (1Pe 1:23–25). From the verses: flesh is the whole man, alive by the breath God gives and mortal when it is withdrawn; nothing in him outlasts the flesh, and what endures is God's word and those who are born of it.

“The Egyptians are man and not God, and their horses flesh and not spirit” (Isa 31:3): flesh is what God is not. So “cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart turns from Yahweh”, but blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh (Jer 17:5–7). Hezekiah said of the Assyrian, “With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is Yahweh our God to help us and to fight our battles” (2Ch 32:8), and the psalmist, “In God I trust; I will not fear. What can flesh do to me?” (Psa 56:5). Jesus told Peter that his confession that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God, was revealed not by “flesh and blood” but by his Father in heaven (Mat 16:16–17). From the verses: man, however strong, is mortal flesh, and to rely on him is to turn from Yahweh; strength and knowledge of the truth are from God.

Job, his skin and flesh wasting, said, “I know that my redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the dust; and after my skin is destroyed, yet from my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19:25–26). David said, “my flesh also will dwell in safety, for you will not abandon my soul to the grave (שְׁאוֹל), nor let your holy one see corruption” (Psa 16:9–10); Peter says David died and was buried and his tomb is still there, so that he spoke of the resurrection of the Christ, whose “flesh did not see corruption” (Act 2:29–31). In Ezekiel's valley flesh and skin came upon the bones and then breath, and Yahweh explains: “I will open your graves and bring you up from your graves, my people, and bring you into the land of Israel” (Ezk 37:6–8, 12). Paul adds that “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God”: at the last trumpet the dead are raised and the living changed, the mortal putting on immortality (1Co 15:50–53), and this at Christ's coming (1Co 15:23). From the verses: the dead are in the grave, not elsewhere; the hope is a bodily resurrection when Christ returns, the raised being then made immortal to inherit the kingdom, as Jesus' own flesh was raised before it saw corruption.

Jesus was “born of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom 1:3), the son of Mary, called the Son of God because the holy spirit, “the power of the Most High”, came upon her (Luk 1:35). “Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same, that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the false accuser (διάβολος), and deliver those who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage”; he was made like his brothers in every respect (Heb 2:14–17), and “in the days of his flesh” he prayed with strong crying to him who was able to save him from death (Heb 5:7). God sent his Son “in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom 8:3). “The word became flesh and dwelt among us” (Jhn 1:14), and the word God speaks is his purpose that goes out and accomplishes what he pleases (Isa 55:11; Psa 33:6); to deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is the spirit of antichrist (1Jn 4:2–3). From the verses: the Son shared the very nature of those he saves, mortal flesh with its trials, so that sin's power, which works in the flesh to death, was overcome in that flesh by his obedience and death; God's purpose was made flesh in a man born of Mary.

The herald of Isaiah carries one message to Zion: “Behold your God!” and “Your God reigns”, with peace and salvation (Isa 40:9; 52:7); the psalm bids Israel proclaim his salvation from day to day and say among the nations, “Yahweh reigns … for he comes to judge the earth” (Psa 96:2, 10, 13). The one anointed with Yahweh's spirit is sent to proclaim good news to the humble and liberty to the captives (Isa 61:1–2). Jesus read that passage and said, “Today this scripture is fulfilled” (Luk 4:18–21); he came “proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom of God” (Mrk 1:14–15) and said, “I must proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God to the other cities also” (Luk 4:43). Philip preached “the things concerning the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ” (Act 8:12), and Paul applies Isa 52:7 to those sent to preach (Rom 10:15). The scripture “proclaimed the gospel beforehand to Abraham, In you shall all the nations be blessed” (Gal 3:8; Gen 12:3). From the verses: the good news the Hebrew verb proclaims is that God will reign, from Zion, over the earth; the gospel of the New Testament is that same message, the kingdom of God promised to Abraham, with the name of Jesus the Christ through whom it comes.

When the glory of Yahweh is revealed “all flesh shall see it together” (Isa 40:5), which Luke applies to the coming of the Christ (Luk 3:6). “From new moon to new moon and from sabbath to sabbath all flesh shall come to worship before me, says Yahweh” in Jerusalem (Isa 66:20, 23). “Be silent, all flesh, before Yahweh”, for he will inherit Judah as his portion in the holy land and choose Jerusalem again, and many nations will join themselves to him in that day (Zec 2:15–17). He will pour out his spirit on all flesh (Jol 3:1), as Peter declared at Pentecost (Act 2:17), and in that day “all flesh shall know that I, Yahweh, am your saviour” (Isa 49:26). From the verses: the earth's peoples, “all flesh”, are to see Yahweh's glory and worship him at Jerusalem when he reigns there, his kingdom on the earth centred on the land and the city he chose.

Yahweh God took one of the man's ribs and closed up the flesh in its place, and built the rib into a woman; the man said, “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”, and “therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh” (Gen 2:21–24). Jesus answers the question of divorce from this: the Creator “made them male and female from the beginning … so they are no longer two but one flesh; what God has joined together, let not man separate” (Mat 19:4–6), and Paul quotes the same words of Christ and the ecclesia (Eph 5:31–32). From the verses: marriage rests on the woman's being made from the man's own flesh in the beginning, a single act of creation that Jesus treats as history; the two become one flesh, kin by God's joining, which man is not to undo.

note: Drafted 2026-11-18. Root key בשׂר, the corpus's and BDB's; no existing entry used it. BDB keys: b.dj.aa verb, b.dj.ab noun בָּשָׂר, b.dj.ac בְּשֹׂרָה, b.dj.ad the wadi Besor (a place: kept as a word, no name file; TIPNR has only Besor@1Sa.30.9, a place, and no personal name of the root). Biblical Aramaic בְּשַׂר is xb.ao.ac (root key בשר), Dan 2:11; 4:9; 7:5; the brief's “also xb.ao.ac” tokens in Hebrew verses are construct spellings of בָּשָׂר, which is why lexicon-support counts 32 uses for the Aramaic word (3 are Daniel's). The Peshitta's בֵּסרָא is SEDRA lexeme 422 (root 289 BSR B); SEDRA's BSR A (lexeme 420, “despise”) is another word, and its tokens (Act 13:41; Tit 2:8) turn up in a plain search for בסר. Syriac ܣܒܪ “preach, gospel” is recorded as a possible cognate only (metathesis argued; SEDRA keeps it under SBR), not as a word of the entry; open question whether to make it one. The two meanings: Arabic keeps both “flesh/skin” and “bring news” under one root, Akkadian and Ge'ez (as found so far) only the news, Ugaritic, Phoenician and Aramaic “flesh”; Lane's lexicographers derive the news from a change in the skin (complexion). Scripture does not show the link, so the root summary says so; no Hebrew verse uses the two together. Greek: the brief's “loans” εὐαγγέλιον and σάρξ are Thayer's Hebrew equivalents, not loans; recorded as renderings. Leads not followed: Ugaritic bšr “bring news” and bšrt “good news” (not checked in DULAT), Sabaean bs²r, Tigre and Ge'ez besrāt, Akkadian bišru “blood relation” (Wiktionary's descendant 𒁉𒄑𒊒, not in Oracc), and Mandaic.
